newsitem.title: USA: Texas utility stranded costs bill voted down.
newsitem.headline: Texas utility stranded costs bill voted down.

text.p: Eleventh-hour legislation allowing Texas electric utilities to use excess profits to pay down stranded costs over the next two years was introduced and quickly voted down in the state legislature on Thursday.

"I'm not hearing of anything that would resuscitate this bill," a utility lobbyist said of the proposal, a last-ditch measure brought before the House State Affairs committee after a deregulation bill was killed earlier this week.
The proposal would have allowed Texas investor-owned utilities to recover potentially millions of dollars in stranded costs from excess profits, lobbyists said.

The proposal also would have allowed the utilities to file plans with the state Public Utility Commission to pay down stranded costs embedded in generating and regulatory assets, according to a draft of the bill obtained by Reuters.
Backed by the Public Utility Commission, the proposal met with stiff opposition from large industrial customers, Texas electric co-operatives and power marketers, lobbyists said.

The legislation was considered a last gasp by electric utilities in the state seeking to avoid rate cuts signalled by the state Public Utility Commission in its recent Central Power & Light Co rate case, lobbyists said.
In the rate case, the utility was ordered to cut retail rates by $27 million this year and by $16 million in 1998 and 1999. The utility has sought a rehearing in the case.

Earlier this week, a compromise electric deregulation bill was pulled from the House State Affairs committee docket by its sponsor, State Rep. Mark Stiles, when it was stalled by opposition from regional electric co-operatives.

An initial Senate bill died after state utilities, power marketers and industrial customers failed to reach agreement on several key issues, including stranded cost recovery and a timeline for opening the retail market to competition.

Lobbyists said there was little hope a rumored special session of the legislature would be called by Gov. George Bush to revisit electric deregulation if the session ends on June 2 without a bill being passed.
